tier_reason: Upgraded B to A on stronger evidence: the Quill README Performance section times g3log against Boost.Log with public harness code (odygrd/logger_benchmarks benchmarks/call_site_latency/benchmark_g3log_call_site_latency.cpp and benchmark_boost_log_call_site_latency.cpp, g3log built from source at pinned commit 8217b08), GCC 14.2, CMake Release with -m64 -march=x86-64-v3, on an Intel Core i5-12600; same harness that gave Iyengar NanoLog its A in wave 11 batch-33. The reckless doc alone would stay B because its g3log wrapper benchmarks/g3log.hpp is missing (404).

corrections.baseline: Boost.Log (asynchronous_sink with text_ostream_backend, auto_flush off) in the Quill logger_benchmarks latency tables; also std::fstream with std::flush after every line and Boost.Log in the reckless doc/performance.md Disk I/O scenario (g3log is not faster than stdio fprintf+fflush there)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Quill README call-site latency, ns, lower is better (Quill v13.0.0 tables): logging numbers, 1 thread, g3log 50th/90th/99.9th 1066/1095/1143 vs Boost.Log 3093/3259/3621, about 2.9-3.2x lower (derived from page data); 4 threads 1188/1402/1936 vs 1582/3148/5050, about 1.3x lower at the median and 2.2-2.6x at the 90th-99.9th (derived from page data); large strings 1 thread 838/856/892 vs 2844/3019/3263, about 3.4-3.7x lower (derived from page data); 4 threads 950/1085/1577 vs 1322/2923/4761, about 1.4x at the median and 2.7-3.0x at the 90th-99.9th (derived from page data). g3log is slower than spdlog (271/296/360 ns, 1 thread) and every other library in those tables except Boost.Log. reckless doc/performance.md, average call latency relative to reckless = 1.00: Disk I/O g3log 30.71 vs fstream 5719.93, about 186x lower (derived from page data), vs boost_log 46.03, about 1.5x lower (derived from page data), but higher than stdio 17.01 and spdlog 23.82; Mandelbrot overhead, 4 worker threads g3log 10.58 vs stdio 15.03, fstream 15.66, boost_log 13.17; 8 threads g3log 3.09 vs stdio 3.70, fstream 4.62 (boost_log 1.82 and spdlog 1.87 lower). First-party README: average call about ~2 us on a 2010 laptop, no baseline named.
corrections.workload: Quill logger_benchmarks call-site latency: each observation is the average of 20 log calls made in a tight loop ('Logging int: {}, int: {}, double: {}' and a variant with a std::string over 35 characters), about 2 ms between observations, 1 and 4 caller threads, backend thread pinned to CPU 5; g3log LOG(INFO) to its default file logger vs Boost.Log BOOST_LOG_SEV to an asynchronous text sink. reckless Disk I/O: average latency of 2048 log calls, each interleaved in the same thread with writing 32 MiB to a new file (64 GiB over 2048 files), every library flushing to the OS per call; plus Mandelbrot total-overhead rows with 4 and 8 worker threads.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Quill tables: GCC 14.2, CMake Release with CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS -m64 -march=x86-64-v3 (logger_benchmarks CMakeLists.txt), C++20, static libraries, g3log built from source at commit 8217b08 per vendor_manifest.json (the README does not say which g3log commit produced the table). reckless doc: gcc 7.3.0, -O3 -ggdb3 -std=c++11 from Tuprules.lua; g3log 1.3.2 library build flags not stated.
corrections.hardware: Quill tables: Intel Core i5-12600 (12th Gen) @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, benchmark-tuned kernel (isolcpus=1-5, nohz_full, mitigations=off). reckless doc: AMD Ryzen 7 2700X 3.7 GHz, 8 cores, SMT off, 32 GiB RAM, Samsung 970 EVO SSD, Linux 4.14.65; its Disk I/O scenario wrote to a WD Red WD30EFRX 3 TB mechanical disk in a Synology DS216j NAS.
corrections.caveats: g3log beats only the slowest or synchronous baselines. In the Quill tables it is second-slowest, ahead of Boost.Log only, and roughly 3-4x slower than spdlog at every percentile; it is absent from Quill's complex-type and throughput tables. Both benchmark pages are written by authors of competing libraries (Quill, reckless). In the reckless doc the 186x figure is std::fstream with std::flush blocking behind a 64 GiB write storm to a NAS mechanical disk, and g3log is slower than plain stdio fprintf+fflush in that same table; across the other reckless scenarios g3log is slow: periodic calls 78.19 vs stdio 43.77, fstream 41.32, spdlog 40.85, boost_log 67.42 (slowest listed), call burst 4.20 vs stdio 2.55, fstream 2.36, boost_log 3.84, Mandelbrot single thread 13.40 vs stdio 12.21, fstream 10.73. The reckless g3log wrapper benchmarks/g3log.hpp is not in the repo (404 at master), so those rows cannot be rebuilt from public code, and they use g3log 1.3.2 with gcc 7.3.0. The README's ~2 us figure is first-party on 2010 hardware with no baseline; the author's worst-case-latency blog post was not reachable. Unlicense public-domain dedication: no patent grant.

notes: Reckless numbers in the record are accurate, but its workload said the 64 GiB were written 'in parallel' (they are interleaved in the logging thread) and its hardware omitted the NAS disk used for the Disk I/O scenario; both corrected.
